content:
I recently wrote up a blog post on Kripke and (generalized) Beth semantics in Lean, which might be of interest to some people here: https://boarders.github.io/posts/beth.html

I am not a Lean expert so would welcome some (friendly!) feedback, in that regard. People might be interested to know that I am using subVerso in order to generate the input needed to show proof state on hover and produce the local proof development page. It would be nice if Verso could support this kind of workflow out of the box, so it could embed in other static site generators.

I also don't know a resource that sets up Beth semantics like this using grothendieck topologies (except a brief mention in Jeremy Avigad's textbook which is what inspired this). I know it is implicit in some of the topos theory literature, but I'd be curious if anyone knows of a source that does something similar. I also don't know a resource that discusses the topology I give in the proof of completeness for Beth semantics. I would imagine it is a special case of something in the topos theory literature, so I'd again be interested in any pointers.

This is way outside my field of expertise, but I was very interested in your construction of "A Kripke frame that refutes the Law of Excluded Middle."

What is the relationship of your code to something like Classical.em and the rest of the classical logic system in Lean? There was some discussion in #general > Make mathlib less dependent on choice for trying to remove classical assumptions from Mathlib. My question is: What does Kripke and Beth semantics "buy us" (so to say) when it comes to working in non-classical systems or trying to do constructive mathematics? In other words, what is the upshot?

i missed this a month ago but your development is very nice! i'm in the process of sketching what a general framework for talking about semantics & logic might look like in cslib, & i might take the liberty of asking for your input when i have something concrete :)) i have defined kripke semantics in my cslib branch (though much less polished than yours), and used it to prove the disjunction property for minimal and intuitionistic natural deduction (in the same spirit as your em example). maybe interestingly i was scared off by the completeness proof, and went via completeness for Heyting algebras (which is easy) — i think the translation effectively pushes the difficult part of the Kripke proof (your prime_extension_avoiding) to an application of (the dual of) docs#DistribLattice.prime_ideal_of_disjoint_filter_ideal.

your Beth completeness proof is very slick i like it a lot — re your reference request this tutorial presents Beth semantics roughly in this way (calling it "sheaf semantics over posets), and chapter 14 of Troelstra & van Dalen's "Constructivism in Mathematics" sets up sheaves on a complete Heyting algebra, and in the previous chapter connects Beth models with the same, which is close but not really what you're looking for. the topology you give strikes me as similar to the one used in this paper to show a completeness result for lambda calculus with sums, which is more-or-less the same as semantic completeness but seen from a computer-science perspective.
